title: ultralarge multimers of von willebrand factor form spontaneous high-strength bonds with the platelet glycoprotein ib-ix complex: studies using optical tweezers
display_name: Ultralarge multimers of von Willebrand factor form spontaneous high-strength bonds with the platelet glycoprotein Ib-IX complex: studies using optical tweezers
abstract: ultralarge von willebrand factor (ulvwf) multimers have been implicated in the pathogenesis of the catastrophic microangiopathic disorder, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. spontaneous ulvwf binding to platelets has been ascribed to increased avidity due to the greatly increased number of binding sites for platelets (the a1 domain) per molecule. to address the mechanism of enhanced ulvwf binding to platelets, we used optical tweezers to study the unbinding forces from the glycoprotein ib-ix (gp ib-ix) complex of plasma vwf, ulvwf, and isolated a1 domain. the unbinding force was defined as the minimum force required to pull ligand-coated beads away from their attachment with gp ib-ix expressing cells. beads coated with plasma vwf did not bind to the cells spontaneously, requiring the modulators ristocetin or botrocetin. the force required to break the ristocetin- and botrocetin-induced plasma vwf gp ib-ix bonds occurred in integer multiples of 6.5 pn and 8.8 pn, respectively, depending on the number of bonds formed. in contrast, beads coated with either ulvwf or a1 domain bound the cells in the absence of modulators, with bond strengths in integer multiples of approximately 11.4 pn for both. thus, in the absence of shear stress, ulvwf multimers form spontaneous high-strength bonds with gp ib-ix, while plasma vwf requires exogenous modulators. the strength of individual bonds formed with gp ib-ix was similar for both ulvwf and the isolated a1 domain and greater than those of plasma vwf induced by either modulator. therefore, we suggest that the conformational state of ulvwf multimers is more critical than their size for interaction with platelets.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Clinical Medicine > Surgery > Orthopedic Surgery

title: rnai-mediated suppression of the mitochondrial iron chaperone, frataxin, in drosophila
display_name: RNAi-mediated suppression of the mitochondrial iron chaperone, frataxin, in Drosophila
abstract: the mitochondrial iron chaperone, frataxin, plays a critical role in cellular iron homeostasis and the synthesis and regeneration of fe-s centers. genetic insufficiency for frataxin is associated with friedreich's ataxia in humans and confers loss of function of fe-containing proteins including components of the respiratory chain and mitochondrial and cytosolic aconitases. here, we report the use of rna-interference (rnai) to suppress frataxin in the multicellular eukaryote, drosophila. phenotypically, suppression of the drosophila frataxin homologue (dfh) confers distinct phenotypes in larvae and adults, leading to giant long-lived larvae and to conditional short-lived adults. deficiency of the dfh protein results in diminished activities of numerous heme- and iron-sulfur-containing enzymes, loss of intracellular iron homeostasis and increased susceptibility to iron toxicity. in parallel with the differential larval and adult phenotypes, our results indicate that dfh silencing differentially dysregulates ferritin expression in adults but not in larvae. moreover, silencing of dfh in the peripheral nervous system, a specific focus of friedreich's pathology, permits normal larval development but imposes a marked reduction in adult lifespan. in contrast, dfh silencing in motorneurons has no deleterious effect in either larvae or adults. finally, overexpression of sod1, sod2 or cat does not suppress the failure of dfh-deficient animals to successfully complete eclosion, suggesting a minimal role of oxidative stress in this phenotype. the robust developmental, biochemical and tissue-specific phenotypes conferred by dfh deficiency in drosophila provide a platform for identifying genetic, nutritional and environmental factors, which ameliorate the symptoms arising from frataxin deficiency.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Clinical Medicine > Surgery > Orthopedic Surgery

title: automatic segmentation of the brain and intracranial cerebrospinal fluid in t 1 weighted volume mri scans of the head, and its application to serial cerebral and intracranial volumetry
display_name: Automatic segmentation of the brain and intracranial cerebrospinal fluid in T1‐weighted volume MRI scans of the head, and its application to serial cerebral and intracranial volumetry
abstract: abstract a new fully automatic algorithm for the segmentation of the brain and total intracranial cerebrospinal fluid (csf) from t 1 weighted volume mri scans of the head, called exbrain v.2, is described. the algorithm was developed in the context of serial intracranial volumetry. a brain mask obtained using a previous version of the algorithm forms the basis of the csf segmentation. improved brain segmentation is then obtained by iterative tracking of the brain csf interface. gray matter (gm), white matter (wm), and intracranial csf volumes and probability maps are calculated based on a model of intensity probability distribution (ipd) that includes two partial volume classes: gm csf and gm wm. accuracy was assessed using the montreal neurological institute's (mni) digital phantom scan. reproducibility was assessed using scan pairs from 24 controls and 10 patients with epilepsy. segmentation overlap with the gold standard was 98% for the brain and 95%, 96%, and 97% for the gm, wm, and total intracranial contents, respectively; csf overlap was 86%. in the controls, the bland and altman coefficient of reliability (cr) was 35.2 cm 3 for the total brain volume (tbv) and 29.0 cm 3 for the intracranial volume (icv). scan matching reduced cr to 25.2 cm 3 and 17.1 cm 3 for the tbv and icv, respectively. for the patients, similar cr values were obtained for the icv. magn reson med 49:872 884, 2003. 2003 wiley liss, inc.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Clinical Medicine > Surgery > Orthopedic Surgery

title: neurologic complications in critically iii patients
display_name: Neurologic Complications in Critically III Patients
abstract: critically ill patients are at risk for neurologic complications [1,2]. many of these complications are part of diagnostic and therapeutic procedures; others are simply manifestations of a more fulminant disease process. neurologic complications may put an end to the expectation of full recovery, and outcome is often poor. neurologic complications in critically ill patients were found in 12% of 175 consecutively studied patients in a medical intensive care unit, but they are likely to be even more prevalent in trauma and transplant units. patients in whom neurologic complications develop during critical illness have twice the length of stay and are twice as likely to die [1]. neurologic assessment in the intensive care unit is limited because many patients are fatigued, sleep-deprived, confused, uncooperative, or heavily sedated and are often treated with neuromuscular blocking drugs. there are large gaps in our knowledge of neurologic complications in critically ill patients. neurologic complications often revolve around three main disturbances: muscle weakness, impaired consciousness, and seizures. this review describes common clinical neurologic complications of a potentially life-threatening illness. coma or failure to awaken a puzzling clinical situation is the failure of patients to awaken after the critical illness has subsided. familiar to intensive care specialists is the patient receiving mechanical ventilation for acute respiratory failure who does not fully recover to a normal level of consciousness after withdrawal of analgesics, sedatives, and neuromuscular blocking drugs. neurologic signs typically associated with metabolic encephalopathy, such as multifocal myoclonus, asterixis, and tremor, are absent. the differential diagnosis in these patients is shown in table 1. despite the use of new short-acting pharmacologic drugs, a common cause of altered consciousness in critically ill patients is related to the previous administration of sedative drugs that have accumulated over days because of diminished clearance or pharmacologic interaction. in many other patients, an anoxic-ischemic insult from brief but significant hypoxemia or hypotension may produce a diffuse encephalopathy that lingers for weeks.table 1: major causes of coma in intensive care unitsin medical intensive care units, failure to awaken often occurs in association with sepsis [3,4]. the central nervous system manifestations in sepsis have not been studied in great detail. patients with acute confusional episodes or any other persistent cognitive abnormality have been said to have "septic encephalopathy." whether a distinct metabolic encephalopathy of sepsis exists after exclusion of confounding factors remains unknown. in progressive multiple organ dysfunction from sepsis, severe hypoglycemia, marked hypotension necessitating increasing doses of inotropic medication, and significant hypercapnia may all contribute to impairment of consciousness. suggested mechanisms for encephalopathy associated with sepsis are decreased cerebral blood flow with similar changes in cerebral extraction ratios, disordered amino acid transport similar to hepatic encephalopathy, microabscesses, and possibly, sustained hypotension, suggesting that septic encephalopathy may be more hypoxemic-ischemic in nature [2]. whether cytokines, such as interleukin-1 or tumor necrosis factor, directly influence arousal remains unresolved. other mimicking clinical conditions, such as multiple small intracranial hematomas, should be excluded and may be found as part of disseminated intravascular coagulation [5]. outcome of patients with septic encephalopathy who remain in coma is poor [4,6]. a possibly underrecognized cause of coma after any type of critical illness is cholesterol embolization. recent arteriographic procedures may be implicated [7,8]. in a retrospective review of pathologic material from patients who died six months after vascular catheterization, the incidence of cholesterol embolization was 25%, with embolization to the central nervous system in 5% of the patients [8]. the clinical recognition of neurologic manifestations of cholesterol embolization may be difficult, and the signs of diffuse encephalopathy, retinal hemorrhages, and transient hemiparesis are not specific. the positive predictive value of systemic manifestations, such as livedo reticularis, purple toes, renal failure, and muscle weakness, may be higher [8]. both muscle and renal biopsy specimens may show stacked, needle-shaped crystals. it has been suggested that muscle biopsy has a high sensitivity for demonstrating cholesterol embolization [8]. by comparison, a frequent cause of coma in a surgical intensive care unit is acute renal failure producing acute uremic encephalopathy. acute uremia occurs in approximately 20% of surgical critically ill patients; conversely, acute dialysis in the hospital is associated with perioperative acute renal failure [9,10]. valvular heart surgery, coronary artery bypass grafting, and aortic aneurysm surgery typically are associated with postoperative acute renal failure, but the incidence is also high in liver transplantation [11,12] and in major surgical repairs complicated by sepsis or involving significant abdominal gastrointestinal exploration and repair. the development of acute uremia in surgical patients dramatically increases the risk of mortality, which approaches 100% if mechanical ventilation is necessary [10]. the most common causes of acute renal failure in surgically ill patients are renal hypoperfusion and nephrotoxic insults. not unexpectedly, left ventricular dysfunction, diabetes, and use of nephrotoxic antibiotics are major risk factors in patients with preexisting renal dysfunction. coma from uremic encephalopathy usually develops gradually from drowsiness, asterixis, and myoclonus to an unresponsive state with virtually no motor response to pain. frontal release signs may be seen, such as marked snout response or brief jerks of retroflexion of the neck after glabellar tapping and grasp reflexes. typically, the cranial nerves remain intact, as in many metabolic encephalopathies. uremic encephalopathy usually is the clear overriding cause of coma when blood urea nitrogen and creatinine have doubled in value, but hypoxemia from significant acute respiratory distress syndrome or increased bilirubin from liver failure may contribute. the effect of dialysis is critical in prognostication. failure to awaken may indicate that hypoxemic, anoxic, or hypotensive events have occurred. the clinical signs of uremic encephalopathy may completely resolve after dialysis, but in many patients in the surgical intensive care unit, a baseline drowsiness persists after dialysis. after dialysis, a dysequilibrium syndrome may occur, but it is rare. the typical presentation includes combative behavior, severe throbbing headache when lying flat, and myoclonic jerks and cramps. the circumstances almost always include rapid dialysis, extreme baseline predialysis blood urea nitrogen, and first dialysis. more dramatic presentations may include cortical blindness and coma preceded by seizures. computed tomography scanning may demonstrate significant swelling. many patients die hours after onset [13,14]. in surgical intensive care units, failure to awaken can be associated with ischemic strokes in multiple arterial territories. this devastating complication frequently occurs after major cardiovascular repairs [15]. patients in coma from ischemic strokes immediately after surgery often have had a significant perioperative event. typically, the level of consciousness fails to improve after washout of high doses of narcotic analgesics and anesthetics. in these patients, a brief but significant hypotensive episode may have been noted during surgery, but the anatomical territories of ischemic stroke, often multiple, in these patients do not fit a typical watershed territory figure 1. other established sources of postoperative ischemic stroke are retained left ventricular thrombus, severe atherosclerosis of the ascending aorta with marked circumferential involvement of most of this segment and protruding atheroma [16], and postoperative atrial fibrillation [17].figure 1: computed tomography scan in a patient with multiple strokes after coronary artery bypass grafting. note hypodensities in both anterior and middle cerebral artery territories.in many patients, microemboli may cause prolonged neuropsychologic abnormalities. intellectual deterioration may vary greatly and become evident after the patients return home [18]. with extensive neuropsychologic testing, there may be a prevalence of 30%, which is much higher than that in ischemic strokes in large cerebrovascular territories. in fact, magnetic resonance imaging scans did not find any detectable change after coronary artery bypass grafts [19]. resuscitation for cardiac or respiratory arrest during any type of critical illness may result in postanoxic-ischemic encephalopathy [20]. comatose patients after cardiac resuscitation may show clinical signs portending a dismal outlook. coma alone has no predictive value in the first three days [20]. certainly, if fixed pupils and myoclonus status epilepticus (brief, persistent, and generalized jerks in limbs and face) are associated with a sustained upward gaze, the probability of a persistent vegetative state and death is high in comatose survivors after cardiac arrest [21,22]. in 40% of comatose patients with myoclonus status epilepticus, computed tomographic scan abnormalities of multiple cerebral infarcts or cerebral edema are demonstrated. it is highly probable that status myoclonus is an agonal phenomenon and should be considered a clinical marker for devastating damage to the brain. patients in coma after cardiac or respiratory resuscitation can be further investigated by somatosensory evoked potentials. the absence of a bilateral cortical somatosensory response (n20 and p27) with a preserved cervical somatosensory response strongly predicts a vegetative state [23]. further management decisions should be influenced by these findings. another population of critically ill patients with a propensity for central nervous system involvement are those who have undergone transplantation, notably liver and heart recipients. after liver transplantation, prompt awakening often signifies adequate graft function. when perioperative sedation has been excluded, failure of patients to awaken after liver transplantation may have several causes. patients with fulminant hepatic failure are prone to the development of increased intracranial pressure from brain edema [24] and during the anhepatic phase may even have a brief surge in intracranial pressure. in an extremely unfortunate situation, brain death is diagnosed postoperatively [24]. typically, recovery from cerebral edema takes days before level of consciousness improves. in approximately 10% of patients after liver transplantation, neurotoxicity to cyclosporine develops as early as three days after intravenous administration [25,26]. an acute confusional state with paranoid behavior, tremors, and speech abnormalities may be seen. some patients become mute, but coma with abnormal motor responses is rare, occurring only if cyclosporine neurotoxicity is not recognized. magnetic resonance imaging changes in the white matter have been reported with severe manifestations of cyclosporine toxicity [25]. seizures may occur in the first postoperative days, and, if nonconvulsive status epilepticus follows, it may be a potential cause of failure to awaken. this phenomenon can be recognized in many patients by waxing and waning alertness, stereotypical behavior, and occasional twitching in the face and limbs. central pontine myelinolysis is a less common cause for failure to awaken in recipients of liver transplants, but it may be underreported [27]. in our series of patients undergoing liver transplantation, we found an incidence of 1% and all presented with stupor. rapid shifts in plasma osmolality and plasma sodium have been implicated [28,29], but the relationship was not evident in our survey of patients with central pontine myelinolysis [30]. central pontine myelinolysis can be confirmed by magnetic resonance imaging, which shows a typical bat- or trident-shaped abnormality on axial t2-weighted images. (the trident shape is explained by relative preservation of the corticospinal tracts figure 2.) central pontine myelinolysis, although dramatic in its clinical and neuroimaging presentation, has a reasonable potential for recovery [31,32].figure 2: axial t2-weighted magnetic resonance image of the pons showing typical trident-shaped high-intensity signal after liver transplantation.intracranial hematomas are uncommon (less than 1%) but have been found more often in patients with associated thrombocytopenia, bacteremia, or fungemia [33]. in some patients, a mycotic aneurysm can be implicated. generally, infectious causes of coma after liver transplantation are uncommon. patients with a transplanted heart generally do well in the perioperative phase. neurotoxicity from immunosuppression (cyclosporine, okt3) is uncommon in the intensive care unit [34-36]. possible reasons are meticulous monitoring of okt3 dosage by determination of the degree of decrease in cd3 cells in okt3 and use of cyclosporine at a later stage rather than induction therapy in many immunosuppressive protocols. patients with cardiac transplants, however, are at particular risk for ischemic stroke [36]. a history of stroke and preoperative carotid stenosis of more than 50% significantly increase the risk of ischemic stroke. after heart or heart-lung transplantation, however, ischemic stroke is most frequently associated with retained thrombi within the graft anastomosis. in summary, multiple causes of coma can be considered in critically ill patients. the setting (medical or surgical intensive care unit) may be important in the differential diagnosis. unexplained coma should be evaluated by cerebrospinal fluid examination and repeat computed tomography scanning, but the decision to perform additional diagnostic tests in patients who are critically ill and become comatose depends on the underlying condition. in many patients, the cause of coma is obvious after careful review of the medical record. particular attention should be paid to acute changes in laboratory values (e.g., major shifts in plasma sodium or osmolality), hypoxemic periods or cardiac arrhythmias documented during recent invasive procedures, and any recent change in medication or dosage. computed tomography scanning should be repeated when initial findings are normal and the neurologic examination is not localizing. cerebral infarcts may become more evident two to three days after sudden neurologic deterioration. the major causes of coma in medical and surgical intensive care units are summarized in table 1. generalized muscle weakness fatigue can be expected in critically ill patients after they have survived their illness. an underlying neurologic abnormality should be considered when the patient is mobilized in a chair but appears considerably weak, when the patient cannot support weight, or when weaning failure cannot be readily explained by previous lung disease or new lung injury. at least three major categories have been recognized: axonal polyneuropathy (critical illness polyneuropathy), typically associated with sepsis; acute steroid myopathy, potentially associated with use of neuromuscular junction blockers; and an as yet undefined prolonged muscle weakness after neuromuscular junction blockers, which may represent a toxic myopathy. (the results of electromyographic and nerve conduction studies are often normal.) the definition of all these syndromes continues to be confusing. many other possibilities should be considered, and in some patients a previously undiagnosed neurologic disorder may have been present that initially appeared with respiratory failure. the differential diagnoses to be considered in patients in medical and surgical intensive care units are listed in table 2.table 2: causes of generalized weaknessaprospective studies of causes of weakness in the intensive care unit are few. polyneuropathy is most commonly a cause of generalized weakness in the intensive care unit ("critical illness polyneuropathy") [37]. the prevalence in intensive care units is not exactly known, but it may occur in 5%-20% of all patients with sepsis and in 50% of patients remaining in the unit more than two weeks [38-40]. polyneuropathy of critical illness is often seen in association with sepsis. factors associated with this type of polyneuropathy include age, extended stay in the intensive care unit, hypoalbuminemia, and hyperglycemia. the clinical features of critical illness polyneuropathy are normal cranial nerve findings, although grimacing may be weak [37,38]. limb weakness is usually severe and more prominent in the distal distribution. areflexia is invariably present. prominent muscle wasting may be observed. pinprick is usually diminished in a stocking-glove pattern. the disorder resolves in a stereotypical manner: improvement in the upper and proximal portions of the lower limbs is followed by successful weaning and later recovery of the distal muscles of the lower limbs. outcome is generally good if the patient survives the critical illness [37]. as expected with axonal regeneration, three to four months is needed for improvement. a recent study found a severe residual functional handicap in 20% of seven-year survivors with polyneuropathy [39]. some patients have persistent weakness of the foot flexors from entrapment neuropathy of the peroneal nerve [37]. compression neuropathy of the peroneal nerve may occur when paralyzed limbs are everted. trochanter rolls can prevent this unnecessary complication. electrophysiologic studies in critical illness polyneuropathy may show typical features of axonal damage, with low amplitudes of compound muscle and sensory nerve action potentials, widespread fibrillation potentials, and positive sharp waves, but nerve conduction velocities are perserved [41]. phrenic nerve conduction is often absent [37,38]. autopsy or sural nerve biopsy specimens show severe axonal degeneration of peripheral nerves, mostly in the distal segments. another important cause of generalized muscle weakness is the use of neuromuscular blocking drugs, particularly pancuronium and vecuronium. most patients recover within days after administration is discontinued, but some remain weak for weeks. the mechanism of weakness is unresolved. careful, repeated studies of the neuromuscular junction have not been done, and findings may be normal despite marked limb weakness. a recent prospective study found that metabolites of vecuronium may accumulate in patients with renal failure, metabolic acidosis, and hypermagnesemia [42]. electrophysiologic data for these patients with prolonged weakness were not available. complete recovery can be expected [42]. the prevalence of prolonged weakness is low; a recent report noted the occurrence in only 1 of 58 prospectively studied patients. it is unclear whether monitoring with a peripheral nerve stimulator can prevent this complication [43]. a well-recognized but uncommon complication of intravenously administered neuromuscular blocking drugs is acute necrotic myopathy, possibly when the drug is given in combination with large doses of corticosteroids (usually up to 1 g/d) [44,45]. the typical patient in whom the complication occurs has status asthmaticus. significant loss of myosin has been reported [45]. the outcome appears to be excellent, but data are limited. recently, a myopathy was described in lung transplant patients. muscle biopsy revealed loss of myosin. all patients received large doses of corticosteroids but no neuromuscular blocking agents, and sepsis did not develop. normal creatine kinase levels virtually excluded rhabdomyolysis as a possibility. the underlying cause of this selective loss of myosin is unclear, nor is it clear whether this represents a new syndrome or a variant of acute steroid myopathy [46]. we found that severe necrotic myopathy was more common than polyneuropathy in liver transplant patients but were unable to further delineate the abnormality [47]. rhabdomyolysis may be a source of weakness in critically ill patients. the most common causes are trauma, ischemia of large muscle compartments from arterial occlusion, and sepsis. myoglobinuria can be found when rhabdomyolysis is massive. many patients have considerable weakness and pain. biceps, quadriceps, and gastrocnemius muscles are tender on palpation and may appear swollen figure 3.figure 3: loss of muscle fibers from necrotic myopathy attributed to weakness caused by rhabdomyolysis.seizures one may suspect that the circumstances surrounding critical illness make patients considerably more vulnerable to seizures, but generalized tonic-clonic seizures are title: analysis of the zebrafish proteome during embryonic development
display_name: Analysis of the Zebrafish Proteome during Embryonic Development
abstract: the model organism zebrafish (danio rerio) is particularly amenable to studies deciphering regulatory genetic networks in vertebrate development, biology, and pharmacology. unraveling the functional dynamics of such networks requires precise quantitation of protein expression during organismal growth, which is incrementally challenging with progressive complexity of the systems. in an approach toward such quantitative studies of dynamic network behavior, we applied mass spectrometric methodology and rigorous statistical analysis to create comprehensive, high quality profiles of proteins expressed at two stages of zebrafish development. proteins of embryos 72 and 120 h postfertilization (hpf) were isolated and analyzed both by two-dimensional (2d) lc followed by esi-ms/ms and by 2d page followed by maldi-tof/tof protein identification. we detected 1384 proteins from 327,906 peptide sequence identifications at 72 and 120 hpf with false identification rates of less than 1% using 2d lc-esi-ms/ms. these included only approximately 30% of proteins that were identified by 2d page-maldi-tof/tof. roughly 10% of all detected proteins were derived from hypothetical or predicted gene models or were entirely unannotated. comparison of proteins expression by 2d dige revealed that proteins involved in energy production and transcription/translation were relatively more abundant at 72 hpf consistent with faster synthesis of cellular proteins during organismal growth at this time compared with 120 hpf. the data are accessible in a database that links protein identifications to existing resources including the zebrafish information network database. this new resource should facilitate the selection of candidate proteins for targeted quantitation and refine systematic genetic network analysis in vertebrate development and biology.

title: fatty acid conjugation enhances potency of antisense oligonucleotides in muscle
display_name: Fatty acid conjugation enhances potency of antisense oligonucleotides in muscle
abstract: abstract enhancing the functional uptake of antisense oligonucleotide (aso) in the muscle will be beneficial for developing aso therapeutics targeting genes expressed in the muscle. we hypothesized that improving albumin binding will facilitate traversal of aso from the blood compartment to the interstitium of the muscle tissues to enhance aso functional uptake. we synthesized structurally diverse saturated and unsaturated fatty acid conjugated asos with a range of hydrophobicity. the binding affinity of aso fatty acid conjugates to plasma proteins improved with fatty acid chain length and highest binding affinity was observed with aso conjugates containing fatty acid chain length from 16 to 22 carbons. the degree of unsaturation or conformation of double bond appears to have no influence on protein binding or activity of aso fatty acid conjugates. activity of fatty acid aso conjugates correlated with the affinity to albumin and the tightest albumin binder exhibited the highest activity improvement in muscle. palmitic acid conjugation increases aso plasma cmax and improved delivery of aso to interstitial space of mouse muscle. conjugation of palmitic acid improved potency of dmpk, cav3, cd36 and malat-1 asos (3- to 7-fold) in mouse muscle. our approach provides a foundation for developing more effective therapeutic asos for muscle disorders.

title: irisin mitigates oxidative stress, chondrocyte dysfunction and osteoarthritis development through regulating mitochondrial integrity and autophagy
display_name: Irisin Mitigates Oxidative Stress, Chondrocyte Dysfunction and Osteoarthritis Development through Regulating Mitochondrial Integrity and Autophagy
abstract: compromised autophagy and mitochondrial dysfunction downregulate chondrocytic activity, accelerating the development of osteoarthritis (oa). irisin, a cleaved form of fibronectin type iii domain containing 5 (fndc5), regulates bone turnover and muscle homeostasis. little is known about the effect of irisin on chondrocytes and the development of osteoarthritis. this study revealed that human osteoarthritic articular chondrocytes express decreased level of fndc5 and autophagosome marker lc3-ii but upregulated levels of oxidative dna damage marker 8-hydroxydeoxyguanosine (8-ohdg) and apoptosis. intra-articular administration of irisin further alleviated symptoms of medial meniscus destabilization, like cartilage erosion and synovitis, while improved the gait profiles of the injured legs. irisin treatment upregulated autophagy, 8-ohdg and apoptosis in chondrocytes of the injured cartilage. in vitro, irisin improved il-1 -mediated growth inhibition, loss of specific cartilage markers and glycosaminoglycan production by chondrocytes. irisin also reversed sirt3 and ucp-1 pathways, thereby improving mitochondrial membrane potential, atp production, and catalase to attenuated il-1 -mediated reactive oxygen radical production, mitochondrial fusion, mitophagy, and autophagosome formation. taken together, fndc5 loss in chondrocytes is correlated with human knee oa. irisin repressed inflammation-mediated oxidative stress and extracellular matrix underproduction through retaining mitochondrial biogenesis, dynamics and autophagic program. our analyses shed new light on the chondroprotective actions of this myokine, and highlight the remedial effects of irisin on oa development.

title: alcoholic polyneuropathy: a clinical and epidemiological study
display_name: ALCOHOLIC POLYNEUROPATHY: A CLINICAL AND EPIDEMIOLOGICAL STUDY
abstract: in the present study, we investigated the frequency of polyneuropathy in a sample of 296 alcoholics who were admitted to the 's. maugeri' medical centre for detoxification from october 1997 to november 1999. results revealed a high frequency of polyneuropathy in the sample under study. the disorder was often clinically asymptomatic and demonstrable only on electroneurographic investigation. significant correlations were found between polyneuropathy, the duration of alcoholism, the type of alcoholic beverage consumed (wine) and the presence of liver disease and macrocytosis.

abstract: the oculocerebrorenal syndrome of lowe (ocrl) is an x-linked human genetic disorder characterized by mental retardation, congenital cataracts, and renal tubular dysfunction. the lowe syndrome gene, ocrl1, encodes a phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate 5-phosphatase in the golgi complex. the pathogenesis of lowe syndrome due to deficiency of a phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate 5-phosphatase in the golgi complex is unknown. we have used targeted disruption in embryonic stem cells to make mice deficient in ocrl1, the mouse homologue for ocrl1, as an animal model for the disease. surprisingly, mice deficient in ocrl1 do not develop the congenital cataracts, renal fanconi syndrome, or neurological abnormalities seen in the human disorder. we hypothesized that ocrl1 deficiency is complemented in mice by inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatase (inpp5b), an autosomal gene that encodes a phosphatidylinositol bisphosphate 5-phosphatase highly homologous to ocrl1. we created mice deficient in inpp5b; the mice were viable and fertile without phenotype except for testicular degeneration in males beginning after sexual maturation. we crossed mice deficient in ocrl1 to mice deficient in inpp5b. no liveborn mice or embryos lacking both enzymes were found, demonstrating that ocrl1 and inpp5b have overlapping functions in mice and suggesting that the lack of phenotype in ocrl1-deficient mice may be due to compensating inpp5b function.

display_name: In Vitro Differentiation of Size‐Sieved Stem Cells into Electrically Active Neural Cells

abstract: size-sieved stem (ss) cells isolated from human bone marrow and propagated in vitro are a population of cells with consistent marker typing, and can form bone, fat, and cartilage. in this experiment, we demonstrated that ss cells could be induced to differentiate into neural cells under experimental cell culture conditions. five hours after exposure to antioxidant agents (beta-mercaptoethanol +/- retinoic acid) in serum-free conditions, ss cells expressed the protein for nestin, neuron-specific enolase (nse), neuron-specific nuclear protein (neun), and neuron-specific tubulin-1 (tuj-1), and the mrna for nse and tau. immunofluorescence showed that almost all the cells (>98%) expressed neun and tuj-1. after 5 days of beta-mercaptoethanol treatment, the ss cells expressed neurofilament high protein but not mitogen-activated protein-2, glial filament acidic protein, and galactocerebroside. for such long-term-treated cells, voltage-sensitive ionic current could be detected by electrophysiological recording, and the intracellular calcium ion, ca(2+), concentration can be elevated by high potassium (k(+)) buffer and glutamate. these findings suggest that ss cells may be an alternative source of undifferentiated cells for cell therapy and gene therapy in neural dysfunction.

title: surgical treatment of medullary thyroid carcinoma*
display_name: Surgical treatment of medullary thyroid carcinoma*
abstract: abstract. cohen, ms moley, jf (washington university school of medicine, st louis, mo, usa). surgical treatment of medullary thyroid carcinoma (minisymposium). j intern med 2003; 253: 616 626. medullary thyroid carcinoma (mtc) is a malignancy of the parafollicular c cells of the thyroid gland. it occurs sporadically or as part of the multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (men 2) syndromes. patients who have inherited a mutation in the ret proto oncogene should have thyroidectomy early in life to prevent formation and spread of this cancer. most patients with sporadic disease present with a palpable neck mass. the diagnosis is made by fine needle aspiration biopsy and by measuring calcitonin levels in the blood. primary treatment consists of surgical resection including a total thyroidectomy, central neck nodal dissection and functional lateral neck nodal dissections. most patients with a palpable primary tumour have nodal disease present at the time of operation, and nodal involvement is often bilateral. adequate resection of the primary tumour and cervical lymph nodes is important to optimize outcome and minimize the risk of recurrent disease. proper handling of the parathyroid glands prevents hypoparathyroidism. following primary surgical resection, more than half of the patients will have recurrent disease with persistent elevation of calcitonin levels. currently, there is no adequate systemic therapy for treating recurrent disease. surgical reoperation or conservative observation are the best available options. diagnostic laparoscopy for liver evaluation is the most sensitive diagnostic test to detect the presence of distant metastases.

title: immunoglobulins and dietary protein antibodies in childhood coeliac disease
display_name: Immunoglobulins and dietary protein antibodies in childhood coeliac disease
abstract: twenty-four children with coeliac disease were compared with a control group, comprising 17 children with a variety of gastroenterological disorders, with respect to serum immunoglobulins and dietary protein antibodies. elevated levels of iga and abnormally low levels of igm were demonstrated in one third of the coeliac patients. antibodies to at least one of eight dietary proteins were found in 50% of coeliac children. three children with raised levels of serum iga and two with deficient igm were re-examined after varying periods on a gluten-free diet. antibodies to dietary proteins had waned and immunoglobulin levels returned to normal in all cases. the raised iga was considered to have resulted from an extensive immunological response to antigens of dietary origin which had entered through the abnormal gut mucosa. it is suggested that igm deficiency was due to specific inhibition of igm synthesis by dietary components which had also entered through the mucosa.
